roof_system: Gray asphalt shingles on a multi-level steep-slope roof (upper roof over a lower porch/side-entry roof). T-lock, 3-tab and dimensional-look shingles appear in different sections.
summary: We documented 13 roof items on this multi-level gray asphalt shingle roof. No interior leaks were reported and nothing we saw looks like an active leak today. Three items matter most: the open, poorly flashed spot where the lower roof meets the wall under the upper eave (#8), the torn and sealant-patched shingles at the upper roof edge (#9), and the cracked or lifted tabs on the front slope (#13). Most of the rest comes down to age: shingles that are faded, losing granules, curled or lifted at the edges (#1, #2, #3, #4, #6, #7), exposed nail heads (#10), a ragged eave with no visible drip edge (#11), a gap between the roof edge and the gutter (#5), and a leaning vent pipe worth resealing (#12).

This roof is late in its service life, and some spots have already been patched with sealant instead of replaced (#9). Strong winds catch lifted and unlocked shingle edges (#2, #4, #13). We suggest repairing the wall transition, the upper eave and the loose front-slope tabs first, then the smaller edge, vent and shingle repairs. Repairs buy time but will not make the roof new again, so it is worth planning and budgeting for a replacement in the next few years.

facts.label: Roof system
facts.value: Steep-slope asphalt shingles, gray, on two roof levels. T-lock, 3-tab and dimensional-look styles appear in different sections.

facts.label: Condition
facts.value: Late in service life, with fading, granule loss and curled or lifted edges. The T-lock style is no longer made.

findings.title: Aged shingles late in their service life
findings.description: The roof is covered with interlocking T-lock style asphalt shingles. This style has not been made for many years, so the roof is likely well past mid-life. The surface looks faded and worn across the field. This style is known for edges that lift in wind, and matching replacement pieces are hard to find. That matters for future repairs and for planning replacement.

findings.title: Shingle lock edges look distorted or lifted
findings.description: Along the right side and lower right of this view, the interlocking shingle edges look wavy and uneven rather than lying flat. Lifted or unlocked edges let wind get under the shingle and catch it, and they let wind-driven rain in. A hands-on check would confirm whether the locks are disengaged or the tabs are cracked.

findings.title: Dark spots of granule loss on shingles
findings.description: There are dark patches on several shingle tabs where the protective granules are worn off or knocked off. Similar spots show near the eaves in other frames (F17, F18). Once the granules are gone, sun breaks down the asphalt underneath and those spots age faster. A hands-on check would confirm whether these are wear spots or impact marks from hail.

findings.title: Possible lifted shingle on lower roof
findings.description: Near the downspout on the lower roof, one shingle edge looks raised or out of line with its neighbors. It also shows in F21. A lifted shingle can catch wind and tear loose, and it lets wind-driven rain get under the course above. A hands-on check would confirm whether it is unsealed, cracked or missing a fastener.

findings.title: Gap between roof edge and gutter
findings.description: Bare fascia shows between the metal drip edge and the back of the gutter. The gutter appears to hang low or has pulled away from the roof edge. The same gap is visible in F21. In heavy rain or snowmelt, water can drip behind the gutter and run down the fascia, which rots wood over time. Raising or re-hanging the gutter, or adding a gutter apron, would direct the water into the trough.

findings.title: Worn 3-tab shingles with curled tab edges
findings.description: Across this slope the 3-tab shingles have lost granules, with dark worn patches and tab edges that sit up and cast shadows. Worn, curled shingles shed water poorly and lift easily in wind. This part of the roof looks near the end of its service life.

findings.title: Damaged shingle tab corner
findings.description: On the right side, one tab corner looks torn or broken where the shingle edge meets the course above. A broken tab exposes the shingle below and the nail line to weather and wind uplift. It should be replaced before it tears further.

findings.title: Open, poorly flashed transition where lower roof meets wall under upper eave
findings.description: Where the lower roof runs up to the wall under the upper roof's overhang, there is a dark open gap with debris. The white metal or trim piece is bent and loose, and there is no clear step or headwall flashing turned up the wall. Water and snowmelt from above can get behind the shingles here, so this spot should be properly flashed.

findings.title: Patched and damaged shingles at upper roof eave
findings.description: At the upper roof's edge, the shingles are torn and patched with smeared sealant, and nail heads are exposed. Sealant patches dry out and crack, and exposed nails let water follow the shank into the deck. These shingles should be replaced and nailed correctly.

findings.title: Exposed nail heads on lower roof
findings.description: Several bare nail heads are visible on the lower roof near the wall. Exposed nails rust and let water run down into the deck. They should be sealed, or covered by correctly lapped shingles.

findings.title: Ragged eave edge with no visible drip edge and exposed nail
findings.description: The upper roof's eave edge is ragged, with layered shingle edges showing and no clear metal drip edge. There is also an exposed nail head near the edge. Drip edge keeps water from wicking back onto the fascia and roof deck, so it should be added.

findings.title: Leaning metal vent pipe; check the collar and flashing seal
findings.description: A metal vent pipe comes through the roof. It has a flashing base and a storm collar, and the pipe leans noticeably. The flashing base looks intact. A leaning pipe can open a gap at the collar, and no sealant is visible there. This joint should be checked and resealed if it is open.

findings.title: Cracked or lifted shingle tabs on the front slope
findings.description: On the front slope, several tabs show dark open gaps. They look like cracked or lifted shingles rather than normal tab slots. Wind-driven rain can get under lifted or split tabs and reach the nails and decking. A hands-on check would confirm how many tabs are loose and whether any are missing.

limitations: This report is based on video footage, not a hands-on walk of the roof. We could not lift shingles, test the seal strips or feel for soft decking.
Flashing hidden under shingles and siding, the underlayment and the roof deck could not be seen. The wall transition (#8) needs a close-up look once the shingles are lifted.
The attic was not inspected, so we could not check ventilation, insulation or moisture on the underside of the decking.
No interior leaks were reported, and no interior inspection was done.
Whether the dark spots (#3) are wear or hail impacts can only be told with a hands-on check.

phases.name: Phase 1: Fix the Key Spots
phases.covers: Properly flash the open transition where the lower roof meets the wall under the upper eave (#8). Replace the torn, sealant-patched shingles at the upper roof edge and nail them correctly (#9). Replace or re-secure the cracked and lifted tabs on the front slope (#13).
phases.when: Next dry day above 40°F, and before snow season.

phases.name: Phase 2: Edges, Vent and Shingle Repairs
phases.covers: Check and reseal the collar on the leaning vent pipe (#12). Re-hang or adjust the low gutter, or add a gutter apron (#5). Install drip edge where it is missing at the upper eave (#11). Re-secure or replace the lifted, distorted and broken shingles (#2, #4, #7). Seal or cover the exposed nail heads (#10).
phases.when: Within the next few months, ideally before winter.

phases.name: Phase 3: Plan for Roof Replacement
phases.covers: Budget for a full tear-off and replacement, since the shingles are worn, curled and losing granules and the old T-lock style is hard to match for repairs. A hands-on check can tell whether the dark spots are normal wear or hail impacts, which can matter for an insurance claim.
phases.when: Hands-on check this season. Replacement within the next few years.

phases.name: Phase 2: Edges, Vent and Shingle Repairs

body: Thank you for letting us look at the roof at 325 S D Street. We took our time up there and wrote down everything we saw. This report is what we found, in plain words.

We think the most valuable thing we can give you is honest information, freely given. Your roof is getting older, and a few spots need care soon, especially before winter. We would rather you hear that from us now than find out from a water stain later.

Whether or not you choose us, we want your roof fixed. The repair plan in this package is yours to keep, no strings attached. Use it yourself, hand it to a contractor, or give it to someone handy. It is written so anyone can follow it. Some of the most helpful steps cost very little.
If you get stuck or a question comes up, give us a call. Advice is always free.

options.name: Option A: Comprehensive Roof Repair
options.subtitle: Repair and seal all 13 documented problems on the existing roof
options.warranty: 1-year workmanship warranty on the areas we repair. There is no manufacturer warranty on repairs to an aged roof. We cannot warrant the old shingles we did not touch.
options.scope: We fix every roof problem in this report. That means rebuilding the open transition where the lower roof meets the wall, replacing damaged and patched shingles, adding edge metal at the eaves, re-flashing the leaning vent pipe, and hand-sealing lifted tabs and exposed nails. This makes the existing roof watertight again, but it cannot reverse the age and granule loss of the shingles.

options.name: Option B: Full Roof Replacement
options.subtitle: Tear off the worn mixed-style shingles and install a new dimensional asphalt shingle roof on all 12.2 squares
options.warranty: 5-year workmanship warranty from R&R Roofing on the full system. Manufacturer limited lifetime warranty on the shingles. Enhanced manufacturer system coverage is available when the manufacturer's matching accessories are used and the job is registered.
options.scope: Tear off all existing shingles down to the deck on both roof levels, and replace any soft decking. Install ice and water shield at the eaves, synthetic underlayment, new drip edge, new step and kick-out flashing at the lower roof-to-wall transition, new pipe boots, ridge vent and dimensional shingles, then haul everything away.

recommendation: We recommend Option B, full replacement, for this roof. Nothing is leaking inside today, and that is good news. But the shingles are late in their life, with fading, granule loss and curled tabs on several slopes. The sections also have three different styles, and one of them, T-lock, is no longer made. That means every repair will be a patch that does not match, and new problems will keep showing up as the old shingles wear out. A tear-off lets us find and fix any soft decking, and it lets us flash the lower roof-to-wall transition correctly from the start. Spending a large repair budget on a roof this worn usually buys only a few years.

Option A is the right choice if you need to hold off on a new roof for a few years or want to plan and save for it. It fixes every problem in this report and makes the roof watertight. Even if you hire no one, please have the open transition where the lower roof meets the wall looked at soon. It is the most likely place for water to get in.

The attic was not inspected. No interior leaks were reported.
